candidates.raw_excerpt: Workers at one of the most advanced AI labs on the planet say they have important information to share — but their employer is preventing them from speaking out. New reporting by the Washington Post revealed a growing divide between workers and management at Google’s DeepMind lab in London, where employees are gagged from letting the public know about their concerns due to a sweeping non-disparagement agreement. Non-disparagement agreements are a kind of legal corporate censorship, by which companies can ensure workers aren’t able to disclose info the company deems to be negative or critical. At the DeepMind labs, it appears to be having its intended effect, scaring workers who say they’d like to be able to keep the public involved as the technology progresses. “This technology is just really consequential and it’s also changing really fast,” one anonymous DeepMind staffer told WaPo . “The public wants to know and deserves to know and often this is the only way that people find out about the harms and potential harms that are happening.” Two of the lab’s staffers told the paper of a discussion group organized by their fellow workers to discuss the implications of the non-disparagement clause, which many signed as a condition for employment. Dozens of employees took part, some of them openly criticizing it with references to the dystopian surveillance state featured in George Orwell’s “1984.” Though questions are swirling over whether Google’s top brass would ever invoke the clause to go after staff — or if Google even could, legally speaking — workers say the agreements go too far regardless. ESA also awarded parallel study contracts to Airbus Defence and Space for NGT and Thales Alenia Space for NGO. candidates.raw_excerpt: Two spacewalking astronauts will finish upgrading the International Space Station's power system today (Nov. 5), and you can watch the action live. NASA astronaut Anil Menon and the Canadian Space Agency 's Joshua Kutryk will install the eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) today, during a roughly seven-hour spacewalk that's scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT). You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 7 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT). NASA astronaut Anil Menon points his camera toward his spacesuit’s helmet visor and takes a selfie during a spacewalk on Oct. 29, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) Today's extravehicular activity (EVA) will be the second in a week for Menon and Kutryk, who installed the station's seventh iROSA during an Oct. 29 spacewalk . That excursion was the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the ISS to date, and the first EVA for a Canadian astronaut since 2019. Today's spacewalk will wrap up an ambitious ISS power upgrade that has taken more than five years to pull off. "The installation job will complete the years-long process that began in June 2021 to augment the space station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts," NASA officials wrote about the EVA in a blog post on Tuesday (Nov. 3) . That's a boost of about 30%. Menon and Kutryk are currently sharing the ISS with five other astronauts — NASA's Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov. Delaney, Kutryk, Teteryatnikov and Watkins arrived at the ISS on Oct. 1, on SpaceX's Crew-13 mission . Dubrov, Kikina and Menon got there in mid-July, aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

candidates.title: Chinese scientists envision the first road on the moon
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Chinese scientists are working to design roads on the moon.

One concept, put forward by a team from Beihang University, envisions a road built from crushed stone that is excavated in situ or sintered on the moon — quite similar to gravel roads on Earth.

"Modern roads began as gravel surfaces, so I think the moon's first road could start the same way," Li Feng, a professor at Beihang University's School of Transportation Science and Engineering, told CGTN.

The moon's environment differs from Earth's — with temperature differences of up to 300 degrees Celsius and a different gravity environment — but the team believes the moon's first roads should meet the same standards: level, solid, durable, economical and feasible.

Li says their goal was to make the technology feasible within 5 to 10 years.

"I think one advantage of our concept is that it's technically more mature, because you don't need to bake large bricks — you only need small crushed stones, either sintered or excavated in situ," Li added.

The team has carried out related research using lunar samples gathered from China's Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 missions.

They have named their conceptual lunar road the moon's "Qinzhidao". The Qinzhidao is generally regarded as ancient China's earliest "highway", built more than 2,200 years ago during the Qin Dynasty.

"We want to pay tribute to that road in ancient China," Li says.

The study was published in January 2026 in the China Journal of Highway and Transport.

candidates.title: Farewell Swift
candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered this morning, bringing the 22-year-old mission to an end. NASA contracted with Katalyst Space in September 2025 to revamp an existing system to try and rescue Swift after increased solar activity caused it to lose altitude sooner than expected. In less than nine months, Katalyst launched their LINK spacecraft to grapple Swift, but attitude control problems scuttled the effort. Swift reentered at 7:39 am EST today over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia at approximately 3.4º N latitude, 98.6ºE degrees longitude. Launched in 2004, Swift studied gamma-ray bursts. With three multiwavelength telescopes, Swift looked at the universe in the visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma-ray bands. In 2017, NASA named it in honor of Neil Gehrels, Swift’s Principal Investigator, after he passed away. Last fall when it became clear increased solar activity would cause Swift to reenter sooner than expected, NASA contracted with Katalyst for $30 million to launch a rescue mission using its LINK spacecraft even though Swift wasn’t designed to be reboosted and didn’t have grappling fixtures. Katalyst’s Kieren Wilson called it an “unprepared but cooperative partner,” good at pointing. The name Swift refers to its ability to quickly repoint itself when a gamma ray burst is detected so the other instruments can study it in the X-ray and UV bands. LINK launched on a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket from Kwajalein Atoll in the Pacific on July 3, 2026 , but soon encountered problems . An unresponsive Reaction Control System (RCS) valve caused LINK to spin up and then a power circuit switch failure doomed the effort. Today NASA credited Swift with broadening “our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system.”

candidates.title: Viasat, SES, and Astranis Win NASA Ka-band Relay Contracts
candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA awarded contracts to Viasat , SES , and Astranis for Ka-band space relay capability concepts, as part of the Space Communications and Navigation (SCaN) program’s Communications Services Project (CSP). Viasat received the largest contract award for $460.9 million. Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. (which is SES Space & Defense) was contracted for $340.4 million, and Astranis was contracted for $264.3 million. The awards are firm-fixed-price contracts, but NASA has the option to award additional funding to advance the work from capability concepts to in-orbit flight demonstrations. The work period runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029. This is part of NASA’s work to replace the aging Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) fleet with commercial services for future missions. TDRS provides information relay services to the International Space Station, Hubble Space Telescope, and other missions. TDRS is expected to support its current missions into the mid-2030s, but it stopped onboarding new missions in late 2024 . According to NASA’s solicitation for the contracts, NASA intends to acquire an end-to-end Ka-band relay service that is backward-compatible with legacy TDRSS users for at least 15 years. The Broad Agency Announcement (BAA) details three phases: a first 6-month phase for concept maturation and risk reduction; an option for up to two years of system integration, flight demonstration and capability verification and validation; and a third option for up to six months of additional demonstration, anomaly resolution, and service validation. Both SES and Viasat received contracts in 2022 when NASA started the CSP to explore future commercial options for TDRS. Here's where and when to look. What is the Taurid meteor shower(s)? Every autumn, Earth plows through streams of debris left behind by Comet Encke, a 3-mile-wide (4.8-kilometer) ice body that orbits the sun once every 3.3 years. These debris streams produce two branches of the Taurid meteor shower : The Southern Taurids, active from Sept. 20 to Nov. 20 and the Northern Taurids, active from Oct. 20 to Dec. 10. As Earth plows through the debris streams, tiny particles slam into our atmosphere at 65,000 miles per hour (104,607 kilometers per hour), producing dazzling streaks of light across the night sky. Both branches of the Taurid meteor shower appear to travel away from a point of origin — or radiant — located in the constellation Taurus , which rises in the southeastern sky during November evenings. The Taurids are known for spawning brilliant fireball meteors, which can flare brighter than Venus as pebble-sized pieces of debris enter and burn up in the atmosphere. When to look for Taurid shooting stars The Southern Taurid shower features two distinct yearly peaks, the first of which occurred on Oct. 14. The second takes place overnight on Nov. 4-5 and is associated with an increase in fireball activity, when up to five meteors per hour could be seen blazing across the sky. The Northern Taurid stream, meanwhile, is expected to peak overnight on Nov. 11-12 with the same predicted hourly rate of up to five meteors per hour streaking across the dark, near moonless sky. candidates.raw_excerpt:
A driver pulls into an underground car park in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province, taps "park" on a smartphone app and is guided directly to a vacant space. If the spot has already been taken, the system automatically recommends another.

Behind this convenience is a technological breakthrough by a research team at the 54th Research Institute of China Electronics Technology Group Corporation (CETC54).

Developed under the name "Xingyuan," the BeiDou micro-base-station system for underground positioning and navigation extends high-precision location services into spaces beyond the reach of satellite signals. The project behind the system has passed a national acceptance review by China's Ministry of Science and Technology, marking an important advance in the country's efforts to build an integrated spatio-temporal network for underground environments.

CETC54 engineer Chen Chong said the system offers more than convenience, opening up new possibilities for intelligent transportation, mining and other sectors and reflecting the expanding use of high-precision positioning technology underground.

Satellite navigation has long faced challenges in underground car parks because satellite signals cannot penetrate underground structures, making accurate positioning on ordinary smartphones difficult and leaving gaps in navigation services.

To address these challenges, the Xingyuan system deploys BeiDou micro base stations underground, enabling accurate positioning and navigation on ordinary smartphones. BeiDou, or the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System, is China's global navigation satellite system.

candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now. The agency issued a request for information (RFI) on Oct. 29 for "in-space servicing" capabilities, which could include boosting Hubble's orbit (which is naturally degrading due to atmospheric drag), or even a mission to "enhance its capabilities" in some way. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 3, 1957: Laika the dog launches with Sputnik 2
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth. Laika was a 3-year-old stray husky-spitz mix from the streets of Moscow, and she was recruited by the Soviet space program for her small size and calm temperament. Unfortunately for Laika, this mission was a one-way trip . The Soviets didn't design a way to bring her back down to Earth. With only 7 days worth of oxygen and a little bit of food on board, Laika launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan with a Russian Sputnik rocket. This was the same kind of rocket used to launch the first Sputnik satellite. Laika was alive when she reached orbit, but she died shortly afterward because the spacecraft's heat shield had broken off. Laika overheated before she had the chance to die of starvation of oxygen deprivation. Laika, the first Soviet space dog to enter Earth orbit, is seen in a training capsule prior to her launch. (Image credit: Roscosmos) Why it mattered Laika has remained one of space history's most beloved and tragic figures. People around the world have dogs as pets who they love as members of their own families. And even nearly 70 years after this flight, it is so heartbreaking to think of Laika on that frightening journey from which she never returned. Laika was one of many different animals that were used in early spaceflight testing. Both the U.S. and Russia launched a number of primates on flights testing early flight technology. Sadly, like Laika, many of these brave creatures did not make it back. Unbelievably, though, some did survive the journey. For example, the chimpanzee named Ham and nicknamed the "astrochimp" survived a 1961 test flight to space. Though, the team behind that flight was so unsure of how it would go that Ham didn't get his name until after it was found that he'd survived his return. Want more space history? candidates.title: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory to burn up this week after more than two decades in space
candidates.raw_excerpt: An illustration of NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory orbiting above Earth. The spacecraft utilized a trio of primary instruments to quickly detect and analyze gamma-ray bursts and other astronomical phenomena for more than two decades. Image: NASA A satellite designed to live two years and named for its speed is ending its life slowly and then with a blistering pace. Unable to steer and unable to observe, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is sinking a few miles a day toward an uncontrolled reentry expected this week. As of Monday, the U.S. Space Force predicted Swift would re-enter Earth’s atmosphere at approximately 3:30 a.m. EST Wednesday, Nov. 4, somewhere within about 21 degrees north or south of the equator — a band that is mostly ocean. According to NASA, most of the roughly 1.6-ton spacecraft will burn up during reentry, when Swift will live up to its name one last time as it slams into the atmosphere at about 17,000 mph. “NASA expects most of the spacecraft to burn up as it travels through the atmosphere, but some components are expected to survive re-entry,” Elizabeth Shaw, an agency spokesperson, said in a statement. “The risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely, approximately 1 in 2,100. NASA and the Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions.” Swift has no engine. Hundreds of miles up, the air is thin but not empty, and each molecule Swift strikes costs it speed, dropping it into denser air that slows it faster still. The sun hastened the fall. Solar activity heats and swells the upper atmosphere, and this cycle produced more drag than expected, NASA said. The completed Swift spacecraft is seen in a clean room at NASA Goddard on Sept. 9, 2003. candidates.title: Residents Horrified as Hackers Seize Control of Emergency Alert System and Warn of Incoming Nuclear Attack
candidates.raw_excerpt: Civilians on both sides of the Russo-Ukranian conflict became victims of some cruel hackers on Sunday, after both Ukraine and Russia’s national emergency-alert apps sent out fake warnings of impending nuclear attacks. According to the Kiev Post , the first hack came on Ukraine’s Air Alert app, a system used to warn millions of civilians of incoming attacks rising from the war with Russia. Air Alert was breached on Sunday evening, with the hackers using the access to broadcast fake alerts about impending radioactive and chemical hazards, on top of vague warnings of civil unrest in Kyiv. One example broadcast in Russian read “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine now. Don’t worry, Oreshnik is on its way,” referring to a type of Russian hypersonic ballistic missile . Officials soon shut the app down, making services unavailable. Soon after, Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry sent out a public announcement on Telegram, warning of a “massive attack” suffered by its own mobile app. In that case, users were warned to begin stockpiling three weeks’ worth of feed and to seek shelter immediately, as nuclear warheads were supposedly screaming toward “every region” of Russia. In Russia’s case, the hackers went even further, blasting their false alarms via regional emergency alert channels belonging to official government accounts. That attack was also short-lived, with Russian officials soon broadcasting that the “situation is under control,” and urging citizens to remain calm and avoid spreading false rumors. Where the hacks originated from is difficult to say. Ukraine’s Air Force reported only that it was fending off “hostile interference,” though any specific actor was unnamed. The fact that both sides were impacted points to a non-involved actor, though with the increasingly absurd conflict running into its fifth year, anything feels possible. candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA's Artemis IV moon mission will be a complicated affair — especially if SpaceX's Starship ends up being the lunar lander. For all of the changing components of the Artemis program over the past several years, one of its most persistent may be the question of how many refueling flights Starship will need to land astronauts on the moon . By summer 2021, it was common knowledge that Starship would require multiple launches to pull off an Artemis moon landing. A Government Accountability Office audit at the time, for example, estimated that it could take up to 16. Earlier this month, a member of the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel said the refueling number could be as high as 22. But that estimate was quickly refuted by SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who posted on his social media platform, X, that it would actually be closer to six or eight. Perhaps an even bigger head scratcher, though, is how the refueling process will be carried out. Where (and when) will Starship's upper stage gas up when it's off planet? NASA released a graphic during a recent Artemis update that outlined an order of operations for the spacecraft on Artemis IV , which will be the program's first crewed lunar landing. The mission will launch a Space Launch System (SLS) rocket with the four Artemis IV astronauts aboard NASA's Orion capsule to high Earth orbit, where they will rendezvous and dock with the Starship lunar lander. (Image credit: NASA) Using Starship's engines, the two spacecraft will burn for the moon, and separate upon their arrival in low lunar orbit. Two astronauts will remain aboard Orion, while the other two will head down to the lunar surface in Starship. candidates.title: Why does Betelgeuse keep fading? The mystery of Orion's giant star
candidates.raw_excerpt: Betelguese, one of the brightest stars in the night sky, has been putting on quite a show lately — but not in the way you might expect. The famous red supergiant in the constellation Orion has been growing noticeably fainter in recent months. Of the 21 brightest stars in the night sky, Betelgeuse is perhaps the most enigmatic. Its changing brightness poses a puzzle: how do the star's pulsations, dust eruptions, and a possible companion contribute to its fading? A giant star with a puzzling name Even the translation of Betelgeuse's name is contentious. For a long time, it was thought to be a corruption of three Arabic words, usually translated as "The Armpit of the Giant." However, other experts in star nomenclature now dispute that interpretation, proposing instead "The Hand of al-Jauzā," with al-Jauzā referring to Orion. Although classified as a red supergiant, Betelgeuse usually appears more orange than red— golden orange or deep topaz. It is one of the most famous stars in its class. Henry M. Neely (1877-1963), for many years a popular lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium , described its restless behavior in his book A Primer for Stargazers : "(Betelgeuse) expands and contracts spasmodically, like an old man with his strength almost entirely spent, panting in the asthmatic decrepitude of old age." The rhythms of a changing star Betelgeuse naturally expands and contracts like a beating heart. As an aging red supergiant, it has a regular pulsation cycle of roughly 430 days: when it expands, its outer layers cool and it dims; when it contracts, they heat up and it brightens. Among first-magnitude stars — the brightest category of stars in the night sky — it is the only marked variable. Its scale is equally remarkable: located 650 light-years away, Betelgeuse is among the largest and most luminous stars of its class, with a luminosity of about 14,000 suns at maximum and 7,600 suns at minimum. candidates.title: 10 asteroid mysteries that Hera will explore
candidates.raw_excerpt: Video: 00:07:25 Hera, the European Space Agency’s first mission for planetary defence, arrives at its target body during November, with the goal of gathering precious data on the kinetic impact method of asteroid deflection – while also solving various scientific enigmas. The small-car-sized spacecraft is headed to the 151-m-diameter Dimorphos asteroid, which orbits in turn around its 780-m Didymos parent. Dimorphos is already historic as the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit changed by human action – when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it on 26 September 2022. DART’s impact caused a brightening visible from distant Earth telescopes, but nobody knows what it did to Dimorphos itself. Hera is going there to perform a close-up crash site survey, to help turn DART’s kinetic impact experiment into a well understood planetary defence deflection technique. Scientists are hoping for bonus science as well. Past spacecraft close encounters have revealed asteroids to be dynamic environments with complex histories – and many outstanding questions still to be answered. candidates.raw_excerpt: Vienna-based startup Tumbleweed is attempting to build an anti-gravity machine—one that looks strangely like a reentry vehicle.   Today, the company announced the closing of a €6.9M ($7.7M) seed round to fund the development of an in-orbit research vehicle—called Oasis Beta—that will be capable of reentering the Earth’s atmosphere, with missions set to begin in 2028. The round will also fund at least three missions in 2027 of Tumbleweed’s Pod payload. Pact VC led the round, with additional participation from Vanagon Ventures, Prototype Capital, EWOR, and a group of angel investors, including SES cofounder Candace Johnson. Return journey: The round comes hot off the heels of Tumbleweed’s first in-space mission. The company sent its first sat— Oasis Alpha —to orbit on SpaceX’s Transporter-17 rideshare in July. On that mission, the sat demonstrated its ability to host microgravity research payloads from four different customers.   Since then, Tumbleweed has seen an influx of demand from customers looking to access microgravity without building a satellite of their own. Tumbleweed specializes in giving space newbies their first ride to orbit. Company officials said Tumbleweed’s decision to build its own reentry vehicle was driven not by a bid to create a best-in-class capability, but by an urge to smooth the path to space (and back) as much as possible for future customers. “It is very consistent with our ethos of space being as much in the background as possible,” CEO Julian Rothenbuchner told Payload. “No one gives a shit about space for us, [so] we’re optimizing for maximum credibility outside of the space industry.” Rothenbuchner said Tumbleweed is evaluating partnerships with other reentry vehicle providers, but building Oasis Beta in tandem to own more of the value chain. He said the Internet is not merely infrastructure, but also shaping new ways of life, driving industrial transformation and fostering intelligent generation.
